sources.note: A commentary in this corpus states the pairing in its own text, usually as 'English (Original)'. These renderings carry a locator and are re-checked by scripts/synthesis_lexicon.py --check, which is why they are the only kind the machine can verify. They are also the only kind that proves a rendering is actually in use here rather than merely available.

Terms this repository already asserted before the lexicon existed. Migrated rather than re-derived, so the seed carries no outside knowledge: every one of these was already in a file under version control. Unverifiable in the sense that no locator points at a commentary using it - but not unsourced.

sources.citation: Dermot Moran and Joseph Cohen, The Husserl Dictionary (London: Continuum International Publishing Group, 2012), A-Z headwords, pp. 23-348.
sources.note: Headwords and their English renderings only, as with dahlstrom-2013: no definition text here or in any file derived from it (L4). Not taken: person and work-title headings, and the 45 headings Moran gives in English alone, since supplying the German would be outside knowledge. Where he prints the article the headword is the bare noun and the article is kept as a form - left-anchored, the article-bearing form matches nothing here. Where his parenthetical lists a second term rather than a variant (Sein, Seiendes) it is dropped, not recorded as a form.

entries.note: The early-Freiburg term. Its presence or absence periodizes, which is the whole point of the sorge ledger - and it is rendered 'concern' in GA 61, the same English word GA 20 and SZ use for Besorgen.

entries.gloss: Care in the mode of dealing with equipment - the ready-to-hand, not other people.
entries.note: Shares the English 'concern' with Bekuemmerung, which is a different term from a different period. A hit on 'concern' does not say which is meant; the German does.
The French limb of the Leib/Koerper distinction, and the entry a Merleau-Ponty lexicon would extend first - he is named 146 times across this corpus and has no commentary of his own in it.

The article is part of the term, and it is what makes it searchable: the bare Man would fire on every English 'man', while 'das Man' occurs 293 times in five commentaries and is always the term. The English 'they' is not searchable at all.

renderings.note: The traditional sense - existentia, that a thing is - which GA 24 is expounding in Kant, not Heidegger's own term. Same word, different concept, and no search can tell them apart.

entries.note: No theme, and the densest unregistered headword in the corpus - the German alone occurs 6,070 times across 23 commentaries. The standing example of why --candidates ranks by density rather than by interest: nobody was going to forget Dasein, but nothing in the registry noticed it was missing either.

entries.gloss: The suspension of the natural attitude's positing. Registered separately from the reduction because the commentaries do not always identify the two.
entries.note: Also spelled Epoche without the accent - 7 hits in one commentary against 94 for Epoché - and that unaccented spelling is the German word Heidegger uses for an epoch of the history of being, registered as epoche-de. The matcher cannot separate the two.

entries.gloss: Heidegger's epoch in the history of being - the sense in play where a text speaks of epochs of metaphysics or of presence. Not Husserl's epoché, which shares the unaccented spelling.
entries.note: Dahlstrom heads the entry 'Epoch (Epoche)' and glosses the German in the same list as Husserl's term, which is how the two were first registered as one. Kept apart here: the id carries the language because both headwords transliterate to the same slug.

renderings.note: The unhyphenated rendering, which is also an ordinary English word - so an absence claim over it needs absent_terms set to the German.
'evidence' in this corpus is overwhelmingly the ordinary English word; the German is the only reliable handle.
The ordinary German sense, which that section names in order to set it aside. A rendering recorded because the corpus contains it, not because it is the right one.

Descartes' term, registered under the wesen theme because gap-007 asks whether the corpus connects it to Husserl's Wesen - and it reaches this corpus only through the Marion commentary, in English. The Latin is not attested here at all, which --attest will say.

The theme registry records that English renderings diverge sharply between translations, so a search keyed to one of them drops whole commentaries. This entry is where that divergence belongs; add a translator field as each attribution is established from a commentary rather than assumed.
Three commentaries, three renderings of one term, all attested. A theme registered with any one of them finds a third of the passages. This entry is the argument for the lexicon in miniature.
